paper_context.research_question: Can a nested attention mechanism (attention-over-attention) that models mutual query↔document attention produce better answer selection for cloze-style reading comprehension than existing attention-based readers, and can an N-best re-ranking step further improve accuracy?
contribution_style: incremental architectural innovation (modular addition to existing attention readers)
simple and lightweight (no additional parameters beyond base model)
main_claims: Introducing an attention-over-attention (AoA) mechanism that places an attention over document-level attentions yields higher-quality document attention and improves answer prediction for cloze-style RC.
AoA Reader outperforms prior state-of-the-art single and ensemble models on CNN and Children's Book Test (NE and CN) datasets by a substantial margin.
An N-best re-ranking strategy using global/local/word-class language-model features further improves accuracy over the base AoA Reader.
AoA Reader is simple in design (adds limited computation and no extra parameters relative to the AS Reader) yet more effective, especially on longer documents.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Shared word embeddings for document and query are beneficial and safe because queries are short and would not learn embeddings well on their own.
supporting_evidence: Section 3: "The motivation of using shared embedding weights is that the length of the query is shorter than the document, and thus the embedding weights will not be fully learned by only using a small amount of training data. By embedding sharing, both the document and query can participate in the learning of embedding..."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If shared embeddings hurt performance (e.g., document and query distributions differ), the reported gains may partly come from embedding choices rather than the AoA mechanism; replication with separate embeddings might change results.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Averaging the document-to-query attentions β(t) across document positions yields a meaningful global importance distribution over query words (β) without re-normalization.
supporting_evidence: Equation 9: β = (1/|D|) Σ_t β(t); text: "we do not apply another softmax to the β, because averaging individual attentions do not break the normalizing condition."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If averaging β(t) produces a poor summary of query importance (e.g., dominated by document positions with noisy β(t)), the AoA-weighted final attention s might degrade performance; alternative aggregation (weighted avg or learned pooling) could be necessary.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Dot product between α (matrix of document-level attentions per query word) and averaged β yields an effective weighted combination (s = α^T β) that captures mutual importance.
supporting_evidence: Equation 10 defines s = α^T β and text explaining it as a weighted sum of α(t) by β(t) weights reflecting query-word contributions.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the simple dot-product weighting is insufficient to model more complex interactions (e.g., cross-token dependencies), performance gains might be limited; more expressive combination functions could outperform dot product.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Improvements reported versus baselines are attributable primarily to the AoA mechanism and the reranking pipeline, given similar base settings.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes the Attention-over-Attention (AoA) Reader: a lightweight neural architecture that (1) computes query-to-document attentions per query word (α), (2) computes document-to-query attentions per document position (β(t)), averages β(t) into β, and (3) forms final document attention s = α^T β. The paper pairs this architecture with an N-best reranking pipeline using global/local/word-class n-gram LMs and K-best MIRA. Empirical claims are that AoA (i) produces higher-quality attended document attention than heuristic merges, (ii) yields consistent accuracy gains on CNN and CBT (NE/CN) over prior attention-based readers, (iii) is parameter-free relative to the AS Reader (no added weights), (iv) benefits long documents more, and (v) can be further improved by N-best reranking (though reranking relies partly on a local LM trained per document). The paper provides formal equations, implementation details, experiments vs published baselines, ablation-style comparisons to CAS Reader (heuristic merging), and analyses by document length and candidate frequency. The reasoning chain is mostly coherent: formal mechanism defined → claimed conceptual advantage (mutual attention) → empirical gains reported. Weaknesses in the argumentative chain include incomplete isolation of the AoA operator (controlled ablations are limited), reliance on published numbers for baselines without full confirmation of identical preprocessing, and use of a non-deployable local LM in reranking which complicates claims about practical improvement.
logical_argument_graph: Problem statement: Cloze-style RC requires modeling mutual document↔query interactions to select an answer word appearing in the document.
Observation: Prior readers compute document-level attention by merging per-query-word attentions via heuristics (sum/avg) or employ heavier architectures with more parameters.
Design decision: Compute per-query-word document attention α(t) and per-document-position query attention β(t) from pairwise match matrix M (Eq.5).
Aggregation choice: Average β(t) across document positions to obtain β (Eq.9); compute final document attention s = α^T β (Eq.10) — the AoA operator.
Operational claim: s yields an ‘attended’ document-level attention that weights individual α(t) according to query-word importance.
Implementation claim: AoA adds computation but no additional trainable parameters compared to AS Reader; thus comparable complexity.
Evaluation claim: AoA Reader improves accuracy vs prior single/ensemble baselines on CNN and CBT NE/CN (Table 3).
Ablation/contrast: AoA outperforms CAS Reader (heuristic merging), suggesting the learned weighting matters.
Reranking addition: N-best decoding + LM-based features + K-best MIRA further boost results (Table 4/5).
Limitation flagged: Local LM trained per-document is not legal in strict test-time settings, affecting deployability of reranking gains.
Conclusion: AoA is a simple, effective architectural augmentation for cloze-style RC, particularly helpful on long documents; reranking yields extra gains but with caveats.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes the Attention-over-Attention (AoA) Reader: given the pairwise matching matrix M between document and query contextual encodings, it computes query-to-document attentions α(t) (column-wise softmax) and document-to-query attentions β(t) (row-wise softmax), averages the β(t) across document positions to obtain β, and produces the final document attention s = α^T β. The model uses shared embeddings and bi-GRU encoders and otherwise mirrors the AS Reader, claiming no additional trainable parameters. Experimental evaluation on CNN and CBTest (NE, CN) shows single-model and ensemble accuracy gains over several baselines. An additional N-best re-ranking pipeline (global LM, local LM trained per-document, word-class LM; weights tuned by K-best MIRA) is reported to further improve CBTest results. The paper argues AoA yields better attended document-level attention than heuristic merges (sum/avg) and scales better to longer documents. Key methodological assumptions include: shared embeddings help, averaging β(t) is a valid aggregation, dot-product weighting s = α^T β captures mutual importance, and reported gains are primarily attributable to AoA and reranking under comparable settings.
logical_argument_graph: Premise: Cloze-style RC benefits from attention distributions over document tokens conditioned on query tokens.
Operation: Compute pairwise dot-product M between document and query contextual vectors.
Operation: Column-wise softmax -> α(t) : document attention per query token (query->doc).
Operation: Row-wise softmax -> β(t) : query attention per document token (doc->query).
Aggregation: Average β(t) across document positions to obtain global β representing query-word importance.
Combination: s = α^T β forms a weighted combination of per-query attentions producing final document attention.
Prediction: Aggregate s over positions sharing same vocab token to produce answer distribution.
Claim: AoA (the β-weighted α) yields higher-quality attended attention than heuristic merges.
Claim: AoA outperforms prior readers on CNN and CBTest benchmarks.
Claim: N-best reranking with LM features further improves accuracy (but local LM trained per-document is not realistic).
Conclusion: AoA is a simple, parameter-free extension of AS Reader that improves accuracy, especially on long documents.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a modest architectural augmentation to pointer-style attention readers for cloze-style reading comprehension: compute the standard query-to-document per-query attentions α(t) (column-wise softmax of pairwise dot-products), compute document-to-query attentions β(t) (row-wise softmax), average the β(t) across document positions to obtain β, then combine as s = α^T β to produce a single "attended" document-level attention used to select answer tokens (sum over positions to map to vocabulary). The authors argue this attention-over-attention (AoA) captures mutual query↔document importance more effectively than simple merge heuristics (sum/avg) and without adding trainable parameters beyond a baseline AS Reader. They empirically evaluate AoA on CNN and CBT NE/CN datasets, reporting consistent single-model and ensemble gains vs. a range of attention-based baselines (AS, CAS, GA, EpiReader, Iterative Attention). They further introduce an N-best re-ranking pipeline: generate N-best answers, refill each into the query, score with global LM, local LM (trained on the test document), and a word-class LM; tune feature weights with K-best MIRA to re-rank. Reranking yields additional accuracy gains, especially on NE where the local LM contributes heavily. The paper's reasoning chain is: (1) prior readers collapse per-query attentions with heuristics that lose per-query importance; (2) measuring document-to-query importance provides weights over those per-query attentions; (3) weighted aggregation (AoA) yields a higher-quality document attention leading to better answer selection; (4) post-hoc reranking using fluency and document-local statistics further filters remaining errors. Strengths include conceptual simplicity, competitive empirical gains, and an interpretable mathematical formulation. Key concerns center on attribution (are gains due specifically to AoA?), the legality and realism of the local LM in reranking, missing controlled ablations (different β aggregations and combination functions), and absent computational/runtime measurements to support the 'no extra parameters / similar complexity' claim. I flag uncertainty where evidence is insufficient (statistical significance, preprocessing parity with baselines, small sample counts in some analysis bins).
logical_argument_graph: P1: Cloze RC benefits from attention mechanisms that produce document-level importance distributions.
P2: Existing approaches combine per-query attentions using heuristics (sum/avg) or pre-defined rules (CAS Reader), which may misweight query tokens.
O1 (operation): Compute pairwise matching M(i,j)=h_doc(i)^T h_query(j); get α(t) by column-wise softmax (query→document); get β(t) by row-wise softmax (document→query).
O2 (aggregation): Average β(t) across document positions to obtain β (query importance vector).
O3 (attention-over-attention): Compute s = α^T β, producing a single attended document-level attention as a weighted combination of α(t) with weights β.
C1 (main claim): s is a higher-quality document attention that yields improved answer prediction versus heuristic merges.
E1 (empirical): AoA Reader outperforms prior single/ensemble models on CNN and CBT NE/CN (Table 3) and shows larger gains on longer documents (Figure 2).
S1 (post-process): N-best reranking with global/local/word-class LMs and MIRA tuning further improves accuracy; local LM drives NE gains.
Uncertainties: some experimental confounds (embedding sharing, preprocessing, hyperparam tuning, ensembling) could account for part of the improvements.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: Reconstructed reasoning: The paper proposes Attention-over-Attention (AoA) as a compositional operator that refines document-level attention by (1) computing a pairwise matching matrix M between contextualized document and query token vectors, (2) forming per-query document attentions α(t) via column-wise softmax (query→document), (3) forming per-document query attentions β(t) via row-wise softmax (document→query), (4) averaging β(t) across document positions to obtain a global query-importance vector β, and (5) combining α and β as s = α^T β to yield a single attended document attention s used for answer scoring (P(w|D,Q) = sum positions si for word w). The authors argue this nests an attention over attentions to explicitly weight per-query attentions, avoiding heuristic merges (sum/avg) and improving focus, especially on longer documents. Empirically, AoA single models and ensembles beat reported baselines on CNN and CBT-NE/CN; an N-best reranking stage (global LM, local LM trained per document, word-class LM) tuned with K-best MIRA further boosts CBT scores. The paper claims simplicity (no extra trainable parameters beyond AS Reader) and similar computational complexity. The authors support claims with numeric comparisons (Table 3), targeted comparisons to CAS Reader (merging heuristics), stepwise ablation-like reranking feature addition (Table 4), and coarse analyses (document-length and candidate-frequency plots). They acknowledge caveats (local LM is trained per test document and thus not legal in strict test conditions) but still report those gains.
logical_argument_graph: L1: Contextual encoders produce h_doc and h_query representations (bi-GRU + shared embeddings).
L2: Pairwise matching M(i,j) = h_doc(i)^T h_query(j) captures token-level affinity.
L3: Column-wise softmax over M yields α(t): document attention per query token (query→document).
L4: Row-wise softmax over M yields β(t): query attention per document token (document→query).
L5: Averaging β(t) across document positions yields global query-importance β (no extra softmax).
L6: Weighted combination s = α^T β aggregates per-query document attentions into a single attended document attention.
L7: P(w|D,Q) computed by summing s over positions of w produces answer probabilities.
L8: Because β is learned from document→query signals, s emphasises query tokens that are important across the document, improving attention focus vs heuristic merges.
L9: Empirical results show AoA > baselines (AS/CAS/GA/EpiReader) on CNN & CBT datasets, indicating effectiveness of s construction.
L10: N-best reranking (global/local/word-class LMs, weights tuned via MIRA) further refines selection by surface fluency/context cues.
L11: Observed larger gains on longer documents and particular candidate-frequency scenarios are offered as diagnostic evidence of AoA's advantages.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes the Attention-over-Attention (AoA) Reader for cloze-style reading comprehension. The architecture computes pairwise dot-product matches M between contextualized document and query tokens, forms per-query document attentions α(t) via column-wise softmax, forms per-document query attentions β(t) via row-wise softmax, averages β(t) into a global β, and computes the final document attention s = α^T β. The model follows the pointer-style prediction (sum attention over positions for candidate words). An N-best re-ranking pipeline (global LM, local per-document LM, word-class LM) with K-best MIRA tuning is used to further boost accuracy. Empirically, AoA single models and ensembles show improved accuracy on CNN and CBTest (NE/CN) vs. several published baselines; reranking yields additional gains, especially on NE where local LM dominates. The paper argues AoA is simple (adds no trainable parameters vs AS Reader) and better on long documents. Evidence in the manuscript supports the mechanism and reported numbers, but key causal attributions (that gains arise specifically from the AoA operator and not other differences) are not fully isolated. The reranking gains rely on a local LM trained per test document—explicitly acknowledged by authors—which is not legal in standard test-time evaluation and thus complicates claims about deployable improvements. Computational complexity and statistical significance analyses are not provided. I characterize claims as supported, partially supported, or overstated below and list concrete concerns and revision actions to strengthen attribution, realism, and reproducibility.

Compute s = α^T β as weighted aggregation of per-query attentions -> final document-level attention (eq.10).
Map document attention to vocabulary probabilities via sum over positions -> answer distribution (eq.11-12).

N-best decoding + refill + LM feature scoring (global/local/word-class) + K-best MIRA tuning -> re-ranked predictions and further accuracy gains (Section 4 and Tables 4–5).

confidence_interval.rationale: I have high confidence in the correctness of the described mechanism and that reported numbers in the manuscript reflect the experiments performed. However, moderate-to-high uncertainty remains about causal attribution (AoA vs other experimental differences), the deployable effect of reranking (local LM issue), and robustness (no multi-seed statistics), so overall confidence in the claimed generality is reduced.

consensus_findings: The manuscript clearly defines an attention-over-attention (AoA) operator: compute pairwise match M, per-query document attentions (α), per-document query attentions (β(t)), average β(t) to β, and combine as s = α^T β to produce final document attention. Equations and architecture diagram make the mechanism reproducible in principle.

Across multiple standard cloze-style benchmarks (CNN and CBT NE/CN) the reported AoA Reader single-model and ensemble results are numerically better than many published attention-based baselines in the literature cited by the authors.

An N-best reranking pipeline using LM-based features (global, local, word-class) with MIRA tuning produces additional gains in the reported experiments; the manuscript documents which reranking features drive gains per category (NE vs CN).
Authors assert AoA adds no additional trainable parameters (no new weight matrices beyond baseline encoders) and is conceptually a lightweight, modular augmentation of existing pointer-style readers.
disagreements: Causal attribution of the accuracy gains to the AoA operator vs. other experiment factors: several reviewers note that gains relative to heuristic-merge baselines (e.g., CAS Reader) are plausible but not conclusively isolated because in-paper controlled ablations (replace only the merge with avg/sum under identical code/hyperparameters/seeds) are missing. Some reviewers treat the provided comparisons to CAS and published baselines as reasonably indicative; others require within-code ablations to accept causal attribution.

Practical significance of reranking: reviewers agree reranking gives numeric improvement in the reported experiments, but disagree on how much of that improvement is deployable. Multiple reviewers flag the per-document local LM used in reranking as 'not legal' at test time; some consider the reranking contribution thus largely illustrative/oracular, while others view it as diagnostically useful provided authors separate legal vs. oracle results.

Sufficiency of evidence for the 'no additional computational cost' claim: some reviewers accept the claim on architectural grounds (no extra parameters in equations) but request empirical runtime/memory/FLOP comparisons; others insist these measurements are necessary before accepting the practicality claim.
uncertainty_hotspots: Lack of tightly controlled ablations isolating AoA: no in-paper experiment that replaces AoA with sum/avg merges (or alternative β aggregations) under identical implementation, training, and seeds to quantify the isolated effect of AoA.

Reranking legality and sensitivity: the local LM is trained per test document in reported reranking experiments (explicitly acknowledged by authors), creating uncertainty about deployable gains. Sensitivity to N-best size, n-gram order, and MIRA tuning is also underexplored.

Comparability to prior baselines: reported comparisons use published numbers from different papers; the manuscript does not fully document whether preprocessing choices (entity anonymization on CNN/DailyMail, tokenization, OOV handling) and hyperparameter regimes match those baselines.

Statistical variability and significance: single-point accuracy numbers are reported without multi-seed averages, standard deviations, confidence intervals or statistical tests, leaving uncertainty whether some reported deltas exceed experimental noise.
Long-document analysis variance: the claim that AoA helps more on very long documents is based on bins with small sample counts, increasing variance in effect-size estimates.

β aggregation design choice: the choice to average β(t) across document positions without re-normalization is not compared empirically to alternatives (weighted pooling, learned pooling, or normalization), so the robustness of that specific design is uncertain.
model_diversity_effects: Ensembling and random-seed variation: ensembles are constructed by averaging four best models trained with different seeds. Without reporting variance over seeds for single models, it is unclear how much of ensemble gains arise from the AoA architecture vs. variance reduction from ensembling.

Encoder and embedding choices interact with AoA: reviewers note shared embedding weights and GRU encoders are implementation choices that could modulate AoA's impact. Different base encoders or separate embeddings might change baseline performance and the measured advantage of AoA.

Reranking features create distinct role-specific effects: global LM favors surface-level fluency and broader corpus statistics (beneficial to CN), local per-document LM amplifies document-local co-occurrence (strongly benefits NE in the reported experiments but is non-deployable as used), and word-class LM supplies syntactic/semantic constraints. The combination changes error profiles and can mask the pure architectural effect of AoA.

Aggregation function variance: the particular non-parametric fusion s = α^T β may behave differently than parametric fusions or iterative mutual-attention variants; diversity of fusion mechanisms could produce different trade-offs between accuracy and computational cost.

Keep the editor in a central adjudication role by asking authors to supply the requested controlled experiments and measurements; the editor can then reassess whether the observed improvements are attributable to the AoA module and whether reranking results are deployable.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the paper's evidential basis and practical claims, please: (1) Add tightly controlled ablations: re-run the model swapping only the AoA aggregation with (a) sum, (b) average, and (c) a small learned-weighted pooling, under identical code, seeds, hyperparameters and preprocessing. human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes Attention-over-Attention (AoA), a lightweight operator that computes mutual query↔document attentions (per-query document attentions α, per-document query attentions β(t), average β, then s = α^T β) and uses that attended document attention for pointer-style answer selection in cloze-style reading comprehension. It reports consistent single-model and ensemble accuracy gains over several published attention-based baselines on CNN and CBT (NE/CN) benchmarks, and an N-best reranking pipeline (global/local/word-class n-gram LMs, K-best MIRA tuning) yields additional improvements. The paper is technically clear and the AoA operator is well specified; however, methodological gaps limit causal attribution, reproducibility, and the deployability of reranking gains.
strengths: Clear formalization and reproducibility of the core operator: pairwise match M, α (query→doc), β(t) (doc→query), β = mean_t β(t), and s = α^T β are explicitly defined (Equations 5–10) and diagrammed, enabling direct reimplementation.

Empirical evaluation on multiple standard cloze benchmarks (CNN and CBT-NE/CN) with single-model and ensemble results showing consistent numeric improvements relative to a range of published attention-based readers.
Conceptually minimal and implementable: AoA is a compact, parameter-light augmentation (no new learned matrices in the manuscript specification) that can be integrated into pointer-style readers.

Reranking pipeline is interpretable: LM-based features (global, local, word-class) with K-best MIRA weight tuning are documented and the manuscript analyzes which features drive gains per dataset/category (NE vs CN).
limitations: Causal attribution not conclusively isolated: the manuscript lacks tightly controlled in-code ablations that replace the AoA aggregation with simple merges (sum/avg) or alternative β-aggregation strategies under identical code, hyperparameters, random seeds, and preprocessing. Thus some or all reported gains over heuristic-merge baselines (e.g., CAS Reader) may be confounded by implementation or tuning differences.

Reranking deployability concern: the reported reranking gains rely substantially on a local LM trained per test document (authors explicitly acknowledge this is 'not legal' in standard test-time settings). This undermines claims about practical, deployable improvement from reranking unless legal alternatives or separated 'oracle' vs 'deployable' results are presented.

Comparability and reproducibility gaps: comparisons to prior work use published numbers from other papers but the manuscript does not fully document whether preprocessing choices (entity anonymization on CNN/DailyMail, tokenization, OOV handling), candidate filtering, or hyperparameter parity were matched; without this, cross-paper numeric comparisons are uncertain.

Missing statistical/variance reporting and computational profiling: primary accuracy numbers are presented as point estimates without multi-seed mean±std, confidence intervals, or statistical tests; claims of 'no extra parameters / similar complexity' are not supported by empirical runtime, FLOPs, or GPU-memory measurements.
open_questions: Please provide within-code controlled ablations where the only change is replacing AoA (s = α^T β) with (a) simple average of α(t), (b) sum of α(t), and (c) a small learned-weighted fusion—trained with identical seeds/hyperparameters—and report mean±std across multiple runs with statistical tests. What are the results?

Recompute reranking experiments excluding the per-document local LM (i.e., present 'deployable' reranking) and, if possible, provide a legal alternative (e.g., a document-conditioned LM trained on training data or cache-style features). How much of the reranking gain remains under deployable settings?

Document exact preprocessing choices (anonymization on CNN, tokenization, vocabulary, OOV handling) and, if feasible, re-run (or cite re-runs of) core baselines (AS Reader, CAS Reader) inside the same codebase/pipeline for a head-to-head comparison. Do the reported gaps persist under identical preprocessing?

Provide empirical computational cost measurements comparing AoA vs the most relevant baseline (AS Reader): training epoch wall-clock time, inference latency per example or batch, peak GPU memory, and total parameter counts. What is the measured overhead (if any)?
Report sensitivity analyses for reranking hyperparameters: N-best size, LM n-gram order, and MIRA tuning stability. How sensitive are reranking gains to these choices?

The manuscript averages β(t) across document positions without re-normalization. Have you tried alternative β aggregation methods (normalized average, weighted/learned pooling, max, secondary attention)? If so, how do they compare?

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper formalizes an Attention-over-Attention (AoA) operator—compute pairwise matches M, per-query document attentions α, per-document query attentions β(t), average β, and combine as s = α^T β—and demonstrates consistent accuracy improvements on CNN and CBT (NE/CN) benchmarks. The AoA operator is simple, parameter-light in the manuscript's specification, and well explained.

Strengths:
- Core operator is precisely defined and easily implementable from the equations and diagram.
- Empirical gains reported across multiple standard datasets with both single-model and ensemble figures.
- Reranking pipeline is interpretable and analyzed by feature contributions (global/local/word-class LMs).

Limitations:
- No tightly controlled within-code ablations isolating AoA vs simple merges (sum/avg) under identical code/preprocessing/hyperparameters/seeds; attribution to AoA is therefore not conclusively isolated.
- Reranking relies heavily on a per-document local LM trained on each test sample (explicitly acknowledged as not legal for standard test-time use), so reranking gains may not be deployable.
- Cross-paper comparisons use published numbers without full documentation of preprocessing/anonymization parity, reducing certainty of head-to-head claims.
- Missing statistical reporting (multi-seed mean±std or confidence intervals) and missing runtime/memory/FLOP profiling to support 'no additional parameters / similar complexity' claims.

Open Questions:
1) Please add controlled ablations that swap AoA for avg/sum (and small learned fusions) with identical code and seeds; what are the mean±std and significance outcomes? 
2) Re-run reranking without the per-sample local LM (or replace it with a legal approximation): how much reranking gain remains? 
3) Specify preprocessing (anonymization, tokenization, vocabulary/OOV handling) exactly; if different from baselines, can you re-run AS/CAS Readers under your pipeline? 
4) Provide empirical timing/memory/parameter-count comparisons between AoA and AS Reader. 
5) Provide sensitivity analysis over N-best size and LM order for reranking. 
6) Have you compared alternative β aggregation (normalized mean, weighted pooling, max, learned attention over β(t))? Results?

Transparency:
Equations, model diagram, and many implementation elements are provided; authors explicitly disclose the local LM legality caveat. Missing are multi-seed statistics, full preprocessing details relative to baselines, and runtime/memory profiling. Release of code, preprocessing scripts, and seeds is recommended to enable replication.

confidence_interval.rationale: Mid-range confidence: I am confident the AoA operator is a clear, implementable idea and that the authors ran the experiments they report. However, because controlled ablations isolating AoA, multi-seed variance reporting, preprocessing parity with baselines, and deployable reranking ablations are missing, the certainty about the magnitude, generality, and deployability of reported gains is substantially reduced. The interval reflects moderate confidence in correctness of the mechanism and experimental signals but substantial epistemic uncertainty about causal attribution and practical impact until requested additional analyses are provided.
